danish.title: Fjortende bog (1812) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Mændene samlede hurtigt deres heste i halvmørket, strammede sadelgjorderne og stillede op i kompagnier. Denisov stod ved vagtmandens hytte og gav de sidste ordrer. Detachementets infanteri marcherede langs vejen og forsvandt hurtigt mellem træerne i den tidlige morgendis, mens hundredvis af fødder plaskede gennem mudderet. Jesaulen gav sine mænd nogle ordrer. Petja holdt sin hest ved bidslet og ventede utålmodigt på ordren til at sidde op. Hans ansigt, der var blevet vasket i koldt vand, strålede, og hans øjne var usædvanligt blanke. Kolde gys løb ned ad hans ryg, og hele hans krop pulserede rytmisk.
»Nå, er alt wæwdigt?« spurgte Denisov. »Bwing hestene.«

Hestene blev ført frem. Denisov var vred på kosakken, fordi sadelgjorderne var for løse, irettesatte ham og steg op. Petja satte foden i stigbøjlen. Hans hest forsøgte som sædvanlig at snappe efter hans ben, men Petja sprang let i sadlen, ubevidst om sin egen vægt, og vendte sig for at se på husarerne, der stillede op i mørket bag ham, hvorefter han red op til Denisov.
»Vasilij Dmitritj, giv mig en opgave! Vær så venlig... for Guds skyld...!« sagde han.
Denisov syntes at have glemt Petjas eksistens. Han vendte sig og kastede et blik på ham.
»Jeg beder dig om én ting,« sagde han strengt, »at adlyde mig og ikke trænge dig selv frem noget sted.«

Han sagde ikke et ord mere til Petja, men red i tavshed hele vejen. Da de nåede skovbrynet, blev det mærkbart lysere over markerne. Denisov talte hvisken med jesaulen, og kosakkerne red forbi Petja og Denisov. Da de alle var redet forbi, satte Denisov sin hest i gang og red ned ad bakken. Glidende på bagbenene gled hestene nedad med deres ryttere ned i kløften. Petja red ved siden af Denisov, og den pulserende banken i hans krop blev stadig stærkere. Det blev lysere og lysere, men tågen skjulte stadig fjerne genstande. Da de nåede dalen, kiggede Denisov tilbage og nikkede til en kosak ved sin side.
»Signalet!« sagde han.
Kosakken løftede armen, og et skud lød. I samme øjeblik hørtes trampen af heste, der galopperede frem, råb lød fra alle sider, og derefter flere skud.

Ved den første lyd af trampende hove og råb piskede Petja sin hest og slap tøjlerne og galopperede fremad uden at agte på Denisov, der råbte efter ham. Det forekom Petja, at det i det øjeblik skuddet faldt pludselig blev lyst som midt på dagen. Han galopperede hen til broen. Kosakker galopperede ad vejen foran ham. På broen stødte han sammen med en kosak, der var sakket bagud, men han galopperede videre. Foran ham løb soldater, sandsynligvis franskmænd, fra højre til venstre tværs over vejen. En af dem faldt i mudderet under hans hests fødder.

Kosakker stimlede sammen ved en hytte, travlt optaget af noget. Midt fra den klynge lød der frygtelige skrig. Petja galopperede hen, og det første han så var en franskmands blege ansigt og skælvende kæbe, mens han klamrede sig til skaftet af en lanse, der var rettet mod ham.
»Hurra!... Drenge!... Vores!« råbte Petja, og idet han gav sin ophidsede hest frie tøjler, galopperede han fremad langs landsbyens gade.

Han kunne høre skydning foran sig. Kosakker, husarer og lasede russiske fanger, der var kommet løbende fra begge sider af vejen, råbte noget højt og usammenhængende. En flot udseende franskmand i blå kappe, uden hue og med et surt rødt ansigt, havde forsvaret sig mod husarerne. Da Petja galopperede hen, var franskmanden allerede faldet. »For sent igen!« fór det gennem Petjas hoved, og han galopperede videre til det sted, hvorfra den hurtige skydning kunne høres. Skuddene kom fra gården ved det godsejersted, han havde besøgt aftenen før med Dolokhov. Franskmændene gjorde modstand bag et risgærde i en have tæt tilgroet med buske og skød på kosakkerne, der trængte sig sammen ved porten. Gennem røgen, da han nærmede sig porten, så Petja Dolokhov, hvis ansigt havde en bleg grønlig tone, mens han råbte til sine mænd. »Gå udenom! Vent på infanteriet!« råbte han, da Petja red op til ham.
»Vente?... Hurra-a-a!« råbte Petja, og uden at tøve et øjeblik galopperede han hen mod det sted, hvorfra skydningen lød, og hvor røgen var tættest.

En salve lød, og nogle kugler peb forbi, mens andre slog imod noget. Kosakkerne og Dolokhov galopperede efter Petja ind gennem gårdporten. I den tætte, bølgende røg kastede nogle af franskmændene deres våben og løb ud af buskene for at møde kosakkerne, mens andre løb ned ad bakken mod dammen. Petja galopperede tværs over gårdspladsen, men i stedet for at holde i tøjlerne viftede han med begge arme hurtigt og mærkeligt, mens han gled længere og længere til den ene side i sadlen. Hans hest, der var galopperet hen til et lejrbål, som ulmede i morgenlyset, standsede pludselig, og Petja faldt tungt ned på den våde jord. Kosakkerne så, at hans arme og ben rykkede hurtigt, mens hans hoved var ganske stille. En kugle havde gennemboret hans kranium.

Efter at have talt med den øverste franske officer, der kom ud af huset med et hvidt lommetørklæde bundet til sit sværd og meddelte, at de overgav sig, steg Dolokhov af hesten og gik hen til Petja, der lå ubevægelig med udstrakte arme.
»Det er forbi!« sagde han med en rynket pande og gik hen til porten for at møde Denisov, der red imod ham.
»Død?« råbte Denisov, der på afstand genkendte den umiskendeligt livløse stilling — så velkendt for ham — som Petjas krop lå i.

»Det er forbi!« gentog Dolokhov, som om det at udtale disse ord skaffede ham en vis tilfredsstillelse, og han gik hurtigt hen til fangerne, der var omringet af kosakker, som var kommet ilende til. »Vi tager dem ikke!« råbte han til Denisov.
Denisov svarede ikke; han red hen til Petja, steg af hesten og vendte med skælvende hænder det blodplettede, muddertilsølede ansigt, der allerede var blevet hvidt, mod sig.

»Jeg er vant til noget sødt. Rosiner, fine rosiner... tag dem alle!« mindedes han Petjas ord. Og kosakkerne så sig forundret om ved den lyd — som et hunds hvin — hvormed Denisov vendte sig bort, gik hen til risgærdet og greb fat i det.
Blandt de russiske fanger, som Denisov og Dolokhov befriede, var Pierre Bezukhov (grev Pjotr Bezukhov).

english.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The men quickly found their horses in the half-darkness, tightened saddle girths, and formed into companies. Denisov stood by the watchman's hut, giving final orders. The detachment's infantry filed along the road and quickly vanished among the trees in the mist of early dawn, hundreds of feet splashing through the mud. The esaul gave orders to his men. Petya held his horse by the bridle, impatiently awaiting the command to mount. His face, freshly washed in cold water, was glowing, and his eyes were especially bright. Cold shivers ran down his spine and his whole body pulsed rhythmically.
'Well, is everything ready?' asked Denisov. 'Bring the horses.'

The horses were brought. Denisov scolded the Cossack because the saddle girths were too loose, then mounted. Petya put his foot in the stirrup. His horse, out of habit, made as if to nip his leg, but Petya leaped quickly into the saddle, unaware of his own weight, and turning to look at the hussars moving up in the darkness behind him, rode up to Denisov.
'Vasili Dmitrich, give me something to do! Please... for God's sake!' he said.
Denisov seemed to have forgotten Petya even existed. He turned to glance at him.
'I ask one thing of you,' he said sternly, 'obey me and don't push yourself into anything.'

He didn't say another word to Petya the entire ride. When they reached the forest's edge, it was noticeably getting lighter over the field. Denisov whispered with the esaul, and the Cossacks began riding past Petya and Denisov. When they had all gone by, Denisov spurred his horse and rode down the hill. Slipping and sliding on their haunches, the horses carried their riders down into the ravine. Petya rode beside Denisov, the pulse of excitement in his body growing constantly stronger. It was getting lighter and lighter, but the mist still hid distant objects. Reaching the valley, Denisov looked back and nodded to a Cossack beside him.
'The signal!' he said.
The Cossack raised his arm, and a shot rang out. Instantly the sound of galloping hooves was heard, shouts broke out from all sides, and more shots followed.

At the first sound of pounding hooves and shouting, Petya whipped his horse and let the reins go slack, galloping forward without heeding Denisov, who yelled after him. It seemed to Petya that at the instant the shot was fired, it suddenly became as bright as noon. He galloped toward the bridge. Cossacks were racing along the road ahead of him. On the bridge he crashed into a Cossack who had fallen behind, but galloped on. In front of him, soldiers—probably French—were running from right to left across the road. One of them fell in the mud under his horse's hooves.

Cossacks were crowding around a hut, doing something. From the middle of the crowd came terrible screams. Petya galloped up, and the first thing he saw was the pale face and trembling jaw of a Frenchman clutching the shaft of a lance aimed at him.
'Hurrah!... Boys!... Ours!' shouted Petya, and giving his excited horse free rein, he galloped forward along the village street.

He could hear gunfire ahead. Cossacks, hussars, and ragged Russian prisoners who had come running from both sides of the road were shouting something loudly and incoherently. A dashing-looking Frenchman in a blue overcoat, bareheaded and with a frowning red face, had been fighting off the hussars. By the time Petya galloped up, the Frenchman had already fallen. 'Too late again!' flashed through Petya's mind, and he galloped on toward the place where the rapid gunfire was coming from. The shots came from the yard of the landowner's house he had visited the night before with Dolokhov. The French were making a stand behind a wattle fence in a garden thick with bushes, firing at the Cossacks crowding at the gate. Through the smoke, as he approached, Petya saw Dolokhov, his face a pale greenish tint, shouting to his men. 'Go around! Wait for the infantry!' he yelled as Petya rode up.
'Wait?... Hurrah!' shouted Petya, and without pausing for an instant, he galloped toward the place where the gunfire was thickest and the smoke was densest.

A volley rang out. Some bullets whistled past; others smacked into something. The Cossacks and Dolokhov galloped after Petya through the gateway into the courtyard. In the dense, wavering smoke, some of the French threw down their weapons and ran out of the bushes to meet the Cossacks, while others fled down the hill toward the pond. Petya was galloping across the courtyard, but instead of holding the reins, he was waving both arms about rapidly and strangely, slipping further and further to one side of his saddle. His horse, having galloped up to a campfire smoldering in the morning light, stopped suddenly, and Petya fell heavily onto the wet ground. The Cossacks saw his arms and legs jerk rapidly, though his head was completely still. A bullet had pierced his skull.

After speaking to the senior French officer—who came out of the house with a white handkerchief tied to his sword, announcing their surrender—Dolokhov dismounted and went over to Petya, who lay motionless with his arms flung out.
'Done for!' he said with a frown, and walked to the gate to meet Denisov, who was riding toward him.
'Killed?' cried Denisov, recognizing from a distance the unmistakable, horribly familiar posture of Petya's lifeless body.

'Done for!' Dolokhov repeated, as if saying the words gave him a kind of grim satisfaction, and he walked quickly to the prisoners, who were surrounded by Cossacks. 'We won't be taking them!' he called out to Denisov.
Denisov didn't reply. He rode up to Petya, dismounted, and with trembling hands turned toward himself the bloodstained, mud-covered face that had already gone white.

'I like having something sweet. Raisins—wonderful ones... take them all!' The words came back to him. And the Cossacks looked around in surprise at the sound—like the yelp of a dog—with which Denisov turned away, walked to the wattle fence, and gripped it.
Among the Russian prisoners rescued by Denisov and Dolokhov was Pierre Bezukhov.
